_comment: Final assessment question bank. 'answer' is the 0-based index of the correct option. Questions marked core:true form the default 20-question assessment. This file is read only by the server; answers are never sent to the browser before submission.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes Total Quality Management (TQM)?
options: A final-inspection programme run by the quality department
A one-time certification project that is finished once the audit is passed
An organisation-wide approach in which everyone continuously improves processes to meet customer needs
A cost-cutting method that focuses mainly on reducing headcount
questions.explanation: TQM is a management approach that involves every function and every person, focuses on customers, manages work as processes and improves continuously. Inspection and certification can be parts of a quality system, but they are not TQM by themselves.

questions.prompt: In TQM, who counts as a 'customer' of the tyre-building department?
options: Both external customers and internal customers, such as the curing department that receives the green tyres
Only the sales and distribution team
Only the drivers who eventually buy the tyres
Only the plant manager, who sets the targets
questions.explanation: TQM recognises internal customers: the next process that receives your output. Tyre building serves curing, and the whole chain serves the external customer.

questions.scenario: Final inspection catches about 95% of blistered tyres before shipment. The production supervisor says this is good enough.
questions.prompt: Why is relying on final inspection alone not enough under TQM?
options: Inspection is the responsibility of a different department, so it is not production's concern
Inspection is always inaccurate and should be removed completely
Customers never notice blisters, so the defects do not matter
Inspection detects defects only after the cost has been incurred, and some still escape; quality has to be built in at the source process
questions.explanation: Inspection remains an important control, but it cannot add quality. Preventing the defect where it is created is cheaper and more reliable than sorting good tyres from bad ones afterwards.

questions.prompt: A defective tyre reaches a customer and results in a warranty claim. Which cost-of-quality category is this?
options: Prevention cost
External failure cost
Internal failure cost
Appraisal cost
questions.explanation: Failure costs that occur after the product reaches the customer (warranty, returns, complaint handling, lost reputation) are external failure costs, usually the most damaging category.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of a Pareto chart?
options: To rank categories by frequency or impact so the team can focus on the vital few
To show how a process changes over time
To prove which root cause created a defect
To show the relationship between two measured variables
questions.explanation: A Pareto chart sorts categories from largest to smallest and adds a cumulative percentage line, helping teams prioritise. It does not identify or prove causes.

questions.prompt: The Pareto chart shows last month's tyre defects (total 240). What cumulative percentage do the top two categories represent?
questions.explanation: Blister (120) + Splice open (60) = 180 of 240 defects = 75%.

questions.scenario: Blisters are the tallest bar on this month's Pareto chart.
questions.prompt: What can you correctly conclude?
options: The root cause of blisters has been proven
All other defect categories can be ignored
Blisters are the largest contributor and a sensible priority for investigation, but their cause still has to be found and verified
Blisters are caused by the operators on the night shift
questions.explanation: A Pareto chart helps you prioritise. It says nothing about why blisters occur; that requires a root cause investigation backed by evidence.

questions.scenario: An inspector wants to record defect types by curing press and shift as they occur, with minimal effort and in a consistent format.
questions.prompt: Which tool fits best?
options: Scatter diagram
Check sheet
Control chart
Histogram
questions.explanation: A check sheet is a structured form for collecting data at the point of observation. Designing it with press and shift columns also builds stratification into the data collection.

questions.prompt: Which tool shows the shape, centre and spread of 100 tread-width measurements?
options: Pareto chart
Histogram
Cause-and-effect diagram
Check sheet
questions.explanation: A histogram groups measurements into intervals and shows the distribution: where the data are centred, how widely they spread and the shape of the distribution.

questions.prompt: You want to explore whether curing time is related to the hardness of cured rubber samples. Which tool should you use first?
options: Scatter diagram
Pareto chart
Check sheet
Cause-and-effect diagram
questions.explanation: A scatter diagram plots pairs of values (curing time, hardness) to reveal a possible relationship between two variables.

questions.scenario: A scatter diagram shows a strong positive association between ambient humidity and blister rate over the last month.
questions.prompt: What is the correct conclusion?
options: Humidity is proven to be the root cause of blisters
Blisters should now be ignored until the weather changes
The scatter diagram is wrong because blisters cannot be measured
The association is worth investigating, but it does not by itself prove that humidity causes blisters
questions.explanation: Correlation is not causation. Both variables could be driven by something else (for example, the season or a coinciding equipment issue). The suspected cause must be tested and verified.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between control limits and specification limits?
options: They are the same thing with different names
Specification limits are calculated from process data; control limits are set by the customer
Control limits are calculated from process data and describe its natural variation; specification limits come from customer or design requirements
Control limits are always wider than specification limits
questions.explanation: Control limits describe how the process actually behaves (voice of the process). Specification limits state what is required (voice of the customer). A process can be in control and still produce out-of-specification product.

questions.prompt: This individuals control chart shows curing platen temperature. Point 17 is above the upper control limit (UCL). What is the most appropriate response?

chart.title: Platen temperature, Press 7 (fictional data, deg C)

options: Treat it as a signal of a possible special cause and investigate what changed at that time
Ignore it, because it may still be inside the specification
Adjust the temperature setpoint after every reading to keep the line flat
Recalculate the control limits immediately so that the point falls inside them
questions.explanation: A point outside the control limits is a signal that something unusual (a special cause) may have occurred. Investigate it. Adjusting after every reading (tampering) increases variation, and widening limits to hide a signal defeats the purpose of the chart.

questions.scenario: The tread-width process has been in statistical control for three months, but the capability index Cpk is 0.8.
questions.prompt: What does this mean?
options: The process is stable and therefore capable; no action is needed
A Cpk of 0.8 means 80% of tyres are within specification
The process is out of control and the control chart must be wrong
The process is stable (predictable) but not capable of consistently meeting the specification, so it needs centring and/or variation reduction
questions.explanation: Stability and capability are different questions. A stable process is predictable, but with Cpk below 1 it will predictably produce some product outside specification. Many organisations aim for Cpk of at least 1.33.

questions.prompt: Variation that is inherent in a process and present all the time, arising from many small sources, is called:
options: Special-cause variation
Common-cause variation
Specification variation
Assignable error
questions.explanation: Common-cause variation is the built-in noise of a stable process. Reducing it requires changing the process (system), not reacting to individual points. Special causes are unusual, identifiable events.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of a cause-and-effect (Ishikawa) diagram?
options: To prove which cause is the root cause
To organise potential causes of an effect into categories so the team can decide which ones to check with evidence
To rank defects by frequency
To track a process over time
questions.explanation: The fishbone diagram structures brainstorming (Manpower, Machine, Method, Material, Measurement, Environment). Its causes are hypotheses until verified with data.

questions.scenario: During a 5 Whys session about a mislabelled tyre batch, someone answers a 'Why?' with: 'The operator was careless.'
questions.prompt: What is the best next step?
options: Check the facts, and ask why the process allowed the error, for example an unclear standard or no error-proofing
Stop the analysis and discipline the operator
Write 'human error' as the root cause and close the report
Skip to a new problem because people issues cannot be solved
questions.explanation: Blaming individuals stops learning. A good root cause analysis asks what in the system (methods, training, design, error-proofing) made the error possible, and checks the answer against evidence.

questions.prompt: Must a 5 Whys analysis always contain exactly five questions?
options: Yes, exactly five, otherwise the analysis is invalid
No, one 'why' is always sufficient
No. Continue until you reach a cause that is supported by evidence and that you can act on; this may take fewer or more than five steps
Yes, and each answer must be a different department
questions.explanation: 'Five' is a rule of thumb. The chain should follow evidence, be revised when evidence contradicts it, and stop at a verified, actionable cause.

questions.scenario: The team suspects a worn curing bladder on Press 4 is causing blisters.
questions.prompt: Which action best verifies the suspected cause?
options: Ask the most experienced operator whether they agree
Replace the bladder and compare blister rate and bladder pressure data before and after over a sufficient number of cycles, with other conditions unchanged
Add a second visual inspector at final inspection
Assume it is true because the fishbone diagram lists it under 'Machine'
questions.explanation: Verification means testing the hypothesis with data: change the suspected cause while holding other factors steady and see whether the effect changes. Opinions and fishbone entries are not verification.

questions.prompt: What happens in the CHECK stage of the PDCA cycle?
options: The countermeasure is selected
The problem is defined for the first time
The change is made permanent in the standard procedures
Results are compared with the baseline and the target to judge whether the change worked
questions.explanation: Plan defines the problem, baseline, target and countermeasure. Do trials it. Check compares results with the baseline and target. Act standardises, adjusts or abandons the change.

questions.scenario: A trial reduced the blister rate on Press 4 from 6.2% to 0.6% over 1,200 tyres with no negative side effects detected.
questions.prompt: What is the appropriate ACT step?
options: Reverse the change so that the original process is restored
Stop monitoring, because the problem is solved for good
Standardise the change (update procedures, PM schedules and training) and keep monitoring to sustain it
Start a completely new PDCA cycle on the same problem without changing anything
questions.explanation: When a change is shown to work, ACT makes it the new standard and keeps checking that the gain holds. Then the team can look for the next improvement.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a CORRECTIVE action (eliminating the cause) rather than a correction or containment?
options: Changing the maintenance system so curing bladders are replaced by cycle count, with deferral approval
Replacing the customer's affected tyres
Adding temporary 100% inspection of Press 4 output
Quarantining suspect tyres in the warehouse
questions.explanation: Correction fixes the immediate nonconformity (replace tyres). Containment stops suspect product from moving on (quarantine, temporary 100% inspection). Corrective action removes the cause so it does not recur.

questions.scenario: A distributor reports a bulge in the sidewall of a new tyre found during pre-fitment inspection.
questions.prompt: What is the appropriate first response?
options: Tell the customer it was probably caused by misuse
Send a free replacement and close the complaint
Wait to see whether more customers complain before doing anything
Treat it as potentially safety-related: escalate and follow the approved safety, traceability and nonconformity procedures, including containment of suspect product
questions.explanation: A sidewall bulge can indicate internal structural separation. Potentially safety-critical issues must be escalated and handled through the organisation's approved procedures, with traceability used to find and contain suspect product. Never make unsupported claims to the customer.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes Kaizen?
options: A large, one-off investment in new machinery
Continuous, incremental improvement that involves everyone, often through many small changes
A quality audit performed once a year
A method of replacing workers with automation
questions.explanation: Kaizen means 'change for the better'. It relies on employee involvement and steady, small improvements that are standardised and built upon.

questions.scenario: A tyre builder repeatedly lifts 25 kg rolls of tread by hand from floor level to the servicer.
questions.prompt: Which Lean concept best describes this condition?
options: Muri (overburden)
Mura (unevenness)
Muda (waste)
Kanban
questions.explanation: Muri is overburden of people or equipment beyond reasonable capacity. It causes injury risk, fatigue and errors, and often leads to Muda (waste) and quality problems.

questions.scenario: Production volume is very low in the first week of each month and requires heavy overtime in the last week.
questions.prompt: Which Lean concept describes this pattern?
options: Muri (overburden)
Muda of transport
Mura (unevenness)
Poka-yoke
questions.explanation: Mura is unevenness in workload or flow. It creates periods of overburden (Muri) and waste (Muda), and the rush at month end often increases defects.

questions.scenario: An operator walks about 25 metres to fetch bead bundles for every tyre built.
questions.prompt: Which type of waste (Muda) is this?
options: Overproduction
Unnecessary motion
Defects
Over-processing
questions.explanation: Walking, reaching and searching that do not add value are motion waste. Point-of-use storage can remove most of it.

questions.prompt: Blister rates seem to differ between curing presses. Which tool separates the data into groups such as press, shift and material batch to reveal such differences?
options: Stratification
Histogram
Pareto chart
Control chart
questions.explanation: Stratification divides data into meaningful groups. Patterns hidden in combined data often appear when the data are separated by machine, shift or material.

questions.scenario: A team removes the splice check from the building cell. Cycle time falls by 8%, but splice-open defects found at final inspection double.
questions.prompt: How should this change be evaluated?
options: A success, because cycle time improved
Not a genuine improvement: it shifts the quality problem downstream and raises the cost of poor quality
A success, because final inspection still catches the defects
Neutral, because cycle time and defects cannot be compared
questions.explanation: Improvements must be judged on the whole system. Moving a problem downstream adds rework, scrap and escape risk, so the net effect is negative.

questions.prompt: Why does TQM emphasise involving operators in improvement work?
options: Because it is required for decoration in reports
Because operators are responsible for all defects
Because managers should not be involved in quality
Because operators have direct process knowledge, and their ownership makes solutions better and more sustainable
questions.explanation: People closest to the work see problems first and understand practical constraints. Involvement builds ownership, which is essential for sustaining standards.

questions.prompt: After a successful improvement, why is standardisation important?
options: It prevents any further changes to the process
It is only needed for audits
It makes the improved method the new baseline, so the gains are sustained and future improvements can build on it
It replaces the need for training
questions.explanation: Without a standard, processes drift back to old habits. A standard is the current best-known method, the foundation for the next improvement.

questions.prompt: Final inspection checked 1,500 tyres last week and rejected 90. What is the rejection rate?
questions.explanation: Rejection rate = rejected units / inspected units x 100 = 90 / 1,500 x 100 = 6.0%.

questions.scenario: 1,000 tyres enter final inspection. 920 pass on the first attempt, 50 pass after rework and 30 are rejected.
questions.prompt: What is the first-pass yield (FPY)?
questions.explanation: FPY counts only units that pass first time without rework: 920 / 1,000 = 92.0%. The 97.0% figure (970 / 1,000) is final yield, which includes reworked units.
